items.body:
Using no synths whatsoever, iconic Mute sound engineer Paul Kendall (Depeche Mode, Recoil, Nitzer Ebb) refines his industrial concrète concept on a second Downwards LP, sampling domestic objects (radiators, flasks, shelves) and emerging with grinding, distorted rhythmic gear that ends up somewhere between Pan Sonic, Phoenecia, General Magic & Pita’s ‘Fridge Trax’.

Kendall cut his teeth in Daniel Miller's Worldwide International studio, engineering for Nitzer Ebb, Wire, Depeche Mode, Recoil and countless others, eventually setting up a short-lived but excellent Mute sub-label The Parallel Series. Following years of close work with Alan Wilder on Recoil material, his 2021 debut for Downwards 'Boundary Macro' made use of an of array of microphones to zoom into various objects' hidden facets, essentially mimicking macro photography by using unusual amplifications to produce rusted rhythms and heavily weathered textures. On ‘AMENACE, goodbye’, he repeats the process but with an array of domestic appliances and objects, leaving pretty much no recognisable trace of the source material by the time he’s finished the process.

Kendall stretches and squeezes his recordings, playing fast and loose with powdery bit-crushed beats and time-stretched blips that are almost too destroyed to make head nor tail of. On opener 'Orgone’, he extracts and loops the recordings to create its own loping rhythm in a mode you might confuse for one of Justin Broadrick's soundsystem-ripping experiments or an unreleased DJ Scud proof-of-concept. Tune in, though, and the full spectrum pops into view: the music's concrète components don't just add texture, they're the glue, the air, the movement itself. By magnifying unheard intimate sounds, Kendall makes the humdrum as menacing as the world beneath the white picket fence in the intro of David Lynch's 'Blue Velvet'. Lock into 'Reset', a whirr of subterranean rumbles and half-hallucinated drones that's as brain-melting as anything on Phoenecia's ketamine-fueled 'Brownout'. Or the fully disorienting 'Diminish', a reduced Pan Sonic-style belter that sounds as if it's being played through the reinforced walls of a bomb shelter.

items.body:
Egil Kalman chases a string of inventive iDEAL LPs with fresh, variegated slants on the space between free jazz, folk, and electronics, weaving modular synths with lithe double bass and Jew’s harp, also performed by drummer Hans Hulbaekmo, across gently tumultuous soundscapes and radiant groovers.

“With Unit of Time, Hans Hulbækmo and Egil Kalman aim to show that we can experience the essence of time through rhythm. How can the perception of time—both for the listener and the performers—be turned completely on its head by rhythm? By zooming in on rhythms from traditional music from around the world, the hyper-focused interplay of free jazz, and the rhythmic structures of just-intoned drone music (which is essentially about resonant intervals built on polyrhythms), these gentlemen create a wholly unique rhythmic universe—a universe where both listeners and performers can lose themselves in a thicket of twisted branches.

As you know, Motvind Records is much about filling out our own record collections, and it’s high time for a drum’n’bass record that you can enjoy on the couch at home. Piercing the Veil by William Parker and Hamid Drake is fantastic, but it’s 25 years old... Now, we finally have another album where the groove button is stuck in the "on" position, and creativity overflows.

"The rhythm section" has long had a supporting role in rhythmic music like jazz, pop, and rock, often overshadowed by a brash saxophonist, lead guitarist, or singer dominating most of the frequency range. In jazz, much happened early on with drummers like Max Roach, Kenny Clarke, and Warren "Baby" Dodds, as well as bassists like Jimmy Blanton, Charles Mingus, and Scott LaFaro. In folk music traditions with strong rhythmic elements, such as those in Africa and Southeast Asia, these instruments have played a more prominent role in shaping the music. But all too often, especially in Norwegian folk music, these instruments have had a rather static function. In my own record collection, I even have an album where the accompanying musicians aren’t credited—it just says, "Ola Opheim, fiddle w/Rhythm."

However, Hans Hulbækmo and Egil Kalman have long been a playful and creative rhythm section, with one foot in free jazz and the other in folk music. They’ve played together in the Marthe Lea Band and other projects, and since last year, they’ve delved into the folk music of Norway and Sweden—all set in an experimental duo format: drums and mouth harp (Hans) meet modular synth and double bass and mouth harp (Egil). They’ve now gone deeper into this, aiming to create an album they can take on tour. Both individually and together, they have explored folk music, jazz, and experimental electronic music. Their projects, such as Hulbækmo & Jacobsen Familieorkester, Skrekk & Guro, Camilla Hole Trio, and Reolô, showcase their diverse musical backgrounds. In this duo project, they draw from rhythmic details in folk music—small elements that form the basis for minimalist compositions full of improvisation.

They have composed and improvised most of the material, including a traditional tune from Setesdal, Filleværen. The album is a good old-fashioned musical journey where all the tracks have distinct characteristics yet are strangely interconnected. The music is also highly visual. Once the record has spun through once, it’s tempting to flip it over again—once you get a taste for good music, it’s hard to stop. And they don’t let the groove dictate everything. Some melodies are interpreted more straightforwardly, but the unconventional instruments they use give the music a different kind of depth. Unusual timbres and sonic phenomena emerge, giving the music a hypnotic quality. Both the listener and the musicians themselves can get lost in the groove, immersed in a rhythmic cosmos.”

items.body:
Previously released on Low Company in 2023, Purely Physical Teeny Tapes reissue the full album from Tarquin Manek, one of the most prolific, distinct and perhaps under-recognised producers in our orbit. If bezonked, subaquatic dub-pop zoners are your thing, anything from The Skaters to Swell Maps, YL Hooi to Carla dal Forno, CS + Kreme to Jac Berrocal, this one’s for you.

The 16th and final number from short-lived yet beloved London shop-turned-label Low Company renders a raft of works made by Tarquin Manek (F Ingers, Kallista Kult, Tarcar) 2013-2020, and shafted in the release schedule until now. Nine songs depict Tarquin in his soggiest songwriting mode, floating over rugged, groggy loops in a rare, non-collaborative form. It’s a captivating self-portrait of an artist who is perhaps best known for his collaborations and work behind the scenes, variously fostering talents from the Naarm (Melbourne) undergrowth such as YL Hooi and Carla dal Forno, the latter of whom was his bandmate in F Ingers alongside Sam Karmel of CS + Kreme, and many of whom would grace Low Company and its cult predecessor Blackest Ever Black. 

A sense of desiccated bliss riddles the bittersweet fantasy tang of ‘Breathing Under Honey’, where Manek sets a course from the bleached coral underfoot on ‘Stones on the Beach’, to a lizard-hipped bossa shuffle on ‘Mirage Game’, via superb bouts of Count Ossie-meets-Spencer Clark whims on ’Submerging Emergency’, thru Hassellian trumpet gargling in the sink on ‘Sea Slug Bender’, to instrumental cyberpunk sea shanty, ‘Age Old Squall’, or coming across Lewis on a jolly with drunken sailors at a late night Berlin bar on ‘Basic Trouble’.

Of course it all hits that crinkled sweetspot for levels of eyes-half-shut perpendicular pop that we’ve come to expect from Low Company and their constellation of affiliates, joining dots between the ahead-of-their-time ‘80s post punk tape oddities that surface on Efficient Space, A Colourful Storm’s febrile dream sequences, to rickety DIY bops from the London mulch.

Laters, Low Company - a proper bunch of sound cnuts.

items.body:
Hot on the heels of their ‘Junglist!’ set, Soul Jazz reload their anthem-studded 2007 comp, packing early-mid ‘90s hardcore and ragga jungle heat by M-Beat & General Levy, Ragga Twins, SUAD, Cutty Ranks x DJ SS.

‘Rumble In The Jungle’ tells the story of jungle’s rapid evolution from mutant hip hop x dancehall in the late ’80s, via hardcore, to its hugely distinctive ragga and jump-up phase of the mid ‘90s. It’s a baga sounds that successive waves of producers have attempted to emulate ever since, but simply doesn’t get better than the OG tackle, as Soul Jazz well know.

The Ragga Twins understandably dominate the set with three bullets, the foundational, acid dancehall rap of ‘Ragga Trip’, sped-up fast rap steez of ‘Illegal Gunshot’, both from 1990, plus the ragga techno of ‘Tan So Back’ (1992), which all sparks so many dances and imaginations BITD. Shut Up and Dance, who issued all the above, are also on board, but with the gummy 2000 garage of ‘No Doubt’, which is hardly a standard, but does show how the sound had muted 10 years later.

The rest is all dead solid as a primer for inquisitive junglists/junglettes, firing General Levy’s alternative national anthem ‘Incredible’ and the murderous DJ SS remix of Cutty Ranks’ ‘Limb By Limb’, beside lesser known but wicked zingers such as DJ massive’s clattering hardcore rufige in ‘Final Conflict’, a deep fried steppa by The Source, and of course X Project’s deadly ramp of Beenie Man & Barrington Levy’s ‘Under Mi Sensi’.

items.body:
Psychedelic sorcerers Nuke Watch return with a definitive blast of improvised studio shenanigans on London’s Sagome, after celebrated turns with TTT, PPM, and patience. Proper outerzone madness, tipped FFO Pekka Airaksinen, Wolf Eyes, Marshall Allen, Sperm.

Expanding from a duo to a trio with the addition of Zack Stafford on wind and electronics, Nuke Watch emulate the effects of some legit Lucy for a particularly skewiff and trippy session on their 8th studio album ‘Fusion’. The key to the LP is in the titular nod to psych jazz and rock hybrids of the ‘70s, where styles began to melt into one another via the extraordinary musical virtuosity of the likes of King Crimson, Tony Williams, and John McLaughlin. But rather than overly intricate key changes and showmanship, Nuke Watch distill a confluence of inspirations - contemporary urban beats, dub, trip metal, outernational trance, US basement noise, raga drone - with an alchemic, imaginative ingenuity they can safely call their own. 

The trio, plus the likes of Daryl Seaver on EWI MIDI and instrument, a la Marshall Allen or Wolf Eyes, giive it hot and sticky with a flow of intuitive ideas best representing a prolific creative practice of open-ended jams. But again, they deftly sidestep the more hoary connotations of psych with a freezer fresh zing and grasp of groove that, just about, lets us know it’s the 2020s, not the 1970s, or at least somewhere along that timeline. This uchronic approach, factored by extramusical prompts from psyops, eschatology, and contemporary political clusterfucks, yields a brace of hypnotic, hallucinatory projections in progression from the swingeing groove and smeared apparitions of the opener, thru the mutant raga of the ‘War Lock’ section, to a properly unbuckled ‘New American Psycho’ movement squirming in space between Sperm and Wolf Eyes’ trip metal.

items.body:
Debut EP of raw drone techno minimalism by London-based Brazilian artist Protocol, doubling as the first entry on his label, interiør, and advised FFO Pan Sonic, CUB, SM-LL, Zhark’s Huren & Kareem.

Recorded ’25-’26, ‘Channel Zero’ feels like staring at snow on an analog tele while the warehouse next door hosts an Eraserhead-themed industrial rave. Ascetic to the bone, it unfurls four starkly reverberant variants of unsteady bass thrum and gloaming atmospheres; emerging from a grayscale blizzard into quaking echoes of early Zhark Records on ‘Lost Signal (Noise)’, and wielding the kicks offbeat against unyielding, gnawing spectral tones in ‘Blind Belief’. We’re most partial to the sleepwalker techno momentum of ‘Electromagnetic Shadow’, pairing gaunt, hovering drone with a pendulous bass march, while ‘Black Snow Cult’ palpitates like Regis & Mønic’s cult CUB duo.

items.body:
Berlin’s lowkey ambient wunderkind follows on the promise of his acclaimed albums since 2018 - solo and as half of OCA - plus production for Kelela, with a lush study in Vibroacoustic therapy intended to help his parents sleep better.

The hour long suite stems from Florian TM Zeisig’s rare visit to his parents’ gaff in rural Bavaria a few years ago, where he discovered they had been using a vibroacoustic mattress - a mattress kitted with transducers or speakers - to aid them in getting some quality kip. Being a good lad, Florian wanted to help his parents in their quest, and spent the next few years developing this soundtrack; a serene 60’ of music resting on a rich bed of layered sub-bass frequencies that surely beckon users to the horizontal. 

Most sensitively tending to this premise, Zeisig takes his role with requisite amounts of conceptual seriousness and gently witted pathos that have come to define his work, as on the critically acclaimed OCA album ‘Aging’ with Yo van Lenz in 2018, and in 2020’s deeply charming ‘Coatcheck’ soundtrack for cloakroom assistants. Working within the “vibroacoustic” framework, his results are typically gorgeous and user-friendly, playing into the space between new age ambient music’s putative therapeutic purposes and its well intended pseudo-science, with a warmly sublime conception of classic ambient music that beautifully resonates with records from Eno to Space Afrika and Midori Takada.

items.body:
On their third album, Henry Birdsey's New England collective submerge windswept Americana in dense, oddly-tuned dronescapes, meditating on folk's origins and future eventualities by stirring banjo and slide guitar phrases with abyssal reeded wails and grungy tape loops.

Best known for his subterranean work with Zach Rowden as Tongue Depressor, Birdsey is one of the New England scene's most prolific operatives. 'Dissection Maps' comes only moments after last year's mossy 'Sewn the Name', and picks up where its predecessor left off. There's a different cast this time around (though how many of the contributors are Birdsey's pseudonyms we can't tell you), but the result is largely similar. Birdsey (or J.M. Eagle) plays banjo, pedal steel, bagpipes and resonator guitar, and takes the lead throughout, jangling over Ann Rowlis' organ, bells and rattles on opener 'Sleeps With Dice', the album's straightest nod to its roots. Things start to disintegrate on 'Singing Loom' when the discernible riffs are traded for magickal sustained tones that seem to melt into one another. It's not clear exactly what instrument is playing or when, but Addison Starkweather-Price's harmonica is a constant, and we're sure we can hear bagpipes in there somewhere.

Reana Doram steps in to add ghostly hammered dulcimer chimes to the gusty 'Dealt in Silver', playing against Grainger Farnsworth's doom-y electric bass punctuations and Rowlis's chilling organ and bells, and she shows up again on the mind-bending closer 'Last Rings', adding galloping rhythms to Ryder Tarbox's fluttering tape loops.

items.body:
A second pressing of last year’s gorgeous fourth and final album from Old Saw, the American Primitive project of Tongue Depressor's Henry Birdsey, riffing on the classic Takoma paradigm with additional ferric washes and layered instrumental drones, huge recommendation if yr into Bruce Langhorne’s ‘The Hired Hand’ or classic work by Daniel Lanois, Laraaji, Pelt, Stars Of The Lid, State River Widening.

'The Wringing Cloth' is Birdsey’s fourth and final Old Saw outing, and ironically it’s also the one that has garnered most amount of critical and commercial success. Old Saw’s shimmering, drone-heavy soundscapes were recorded on 1/4" tape at various locations in New England over the last few years and are once again paired with evocative black and white imagery from photographer Dylan Hausthor, whose landscapes somehow perfectly capture the timeless, widescreen appeal of the music inside.

Birdsey's pedal, lap steel and resonator are at the core of each track, but the album also features Old Saw’s usual personnel; Harper Reed on nylon string guitar and banjo, Ira Dorset on fiddle and bowed strings, Ann Rowlis on reed organ and harmonium, Jim Cutler on telecaster, Addison Starkweather-Price on bass, and Peter Catchpole on metal objects and power hammer. That lap steel lends the music its stylistic anchor, taking us through decades of American folk before gently fraying at the edges. Birdsey's application of classical minimalism - the themes that surge through his work with Zach Rowden as Tongue Depressor - is still somehow present here, especially as the record pulls into its second side and the shimmering country-fied atmosphere is pierced with bell-like sounds, but the overall mood and flavour of the record is distinctly easy on the ear and timeless in its appeal.

As the label put it, “What has always been uncanny about this music is that it arrives in a state at once familiar and obscured, like a memory weighed down with sensory information but no identifying details to place it. The Wringing Cloth walks off further into that geographical dream without time or language, until it’s just a speck of light….”

items.body:
The sublime spirit of Satie endures in Yumiko Morioka’s 1987 landmark of Japanese ambient and modern classical, originally ushered at a time when she was moonlighting in pop songwriting for male idol singers, and has been known to trade for triple figures, even on its 2020 repress. Simply beautiful music FFO John Adams, Brian Eno, Erik Satie.

"Recorded on a Bösendorfer grand piano, much of Resonance was made in an attempt to soothe her creative soul. Constructed from unwritten improvisations with additional instrumentation added later, Resonance explores the space between notes. As such, it's a record that feels open and inviting, permeated throughout with a sense of confident serenity.

The sparse, delicately played notes are allowed to reverberate and echo through the spaces between themselves, giving each track a feeling of both grandeur and intimacy. Like the great pioneers of classical and ambient music, there's a timelessness to Resonance - a comforting, familiar feeling, as if these melodies have always existed.

Resonance drew influence from the popular environmental music culture prevalent in Japan during the late 80s, but it was also heavily inspired by Western musicians such as the avant-garde Parisian composer Erik Satie. Listening today, it still feels fresh and pertinent; a warm, contemplative reflection of a travelled woman."

items.body:
Music From Memory chase their cherished survey of 90s ambient techno with a sparkling set of its Japanese echoes little known beyond its domestic market compiled by Jamie Tiller (RIP) and Eiji Taniguchi - consider it a guided tour to a parallel dimension, primed for the gouch out and lucid dreaming.

Flush with fluttering arps and sanguine grooves, ’Virtual Dreams II - Ambient Explorations 1993-1999’ scans a familiar yet oddly distant sound adjacent to the formative sounds of Warp’s AI series and a whole cohort of ‘90s Western producers. Harvested from Music From Memory’s vast shelves, they introduce the lay ambient fan to a raft of names hardly known beyond their homeland, who still float the imagination to the horizontal and sublime with their contribution to a double refractive dialogue of electronic music influence mutated in translation between East and West since the ‘70s.

Smooth around the edges and clear-eyed in their quest for lushness, all 13 artists share a blissed pathos and effortlessness of execution that will see this set travel to collections across the world. In sequence from the nine minutes of near beat-less burble to ‘Blown Fruit’ by Dub Squad, and thru the twelve minute evocation of Eno or Vangelis’ Bladerunner score in Buddhastick Transparent’s ‘Eras (666)’, they limn a emotive and gently arc taking in Red Planet synth whistles and tactful acid squirm of Akio / Okihide’s ‘Phoenix At Desert’, the chiming carillon of Ambient 7’s ‘Escape’ recalling early Bedouin Ascent and Orbital, 

Yukihiro Fukutomi’s centrepiece ‘5 Blind Boys’ can be heard to bridge the prevailing influence of Japanese environmental ambient with its new green shoots in the ’90s, whilst the likes of Web with a slinky ‘The Cycle of Seasons’ remind to analogs in early Dave Mousing and The Black Dog, along with the air-stepping bliss out ‘Pause’ by Katsuya Hironaka. Fans of Susumu Yokota’s early ‘90s gliders will be in their element with Riow Arai’s shine-eyed ’1969’, and likewise fall for the string laden sashay of ‘Sbow Bird’ by Modern Living, and the oh so demure Carl Craig-via-Paddy McAloon sentiment of ‘Poisson D’Avril (Galaxy Dub)’ by Missing Project. Trust it would take years and wads of dosh to source all this stuff yourself, let MFM do the hard work for ya.

items.body:
FELT survey Copenhagen's contemporary jazz scene with RMC graduate Vincent Yuen Ruiz’s intimate and strikingly minimal rendition of stifled percussion, spacious piano and precise double bass work, tipped FFO of The Necks x Talk Talk, naturally.

Ruiz is a seasoned jazz player who's also nursed a parallel reputation as a post-rocker, formerly playing bass in Plaistow. And it's this knowledge of a world outside of jazz that gives 'Trio' its edge. It's not a post-rock record, by any means, but it's not pure jazz either - or at least, it doesn't sound as if it's confined by the aesthetic. The ensemble formed in 2019, but their last record together, 2021's 'Le seul salut que je connaisse', was recorded as a six-piece. Ruiz strips the sound to its bare bones on 'Trio', relying on unusual percussive sounds (provided by drummer Anders Vestergaard) to fill in some of the gaps. And although Rasmus Kjær takes a de facto lead roll on piano, it's the rhythm section, commanded by Ruiz on double bass, that makes 'Trio' so fascinating.

There's an almost meditative sense of calm to opener 'Choral', with Vestergaard's bowed cymbal tones providing a neat bed for Kjær's Bach and Ravel-inspired flourishes. The tension is only released when Ruiz's soft bass enters the frame, played somewhere between improvisation and composition, minimalism and decelerated chamber jazz. Just as he slimmed down his ensemble, Ruiz slims down the pieces themselves, condensing and distilling his ideas so the record never gets busy, or outstays its welcome. Just head to the  central piece 'Weaving', beautifully balancing its measured piano with Vestergaard's odd flurries of percussion that sometimes appear for just a second.

We can hear post-rock - particularly the variety that Talk Talk perfected - but our brains are also directed into filling in the gaps. 'Trio' is an album that lives and dies on its pauses, focusing on decaying notes and echoing rhythms in all their quiet beauty.

items.body:
Downbeat and deep house mavericks, Steve Cobby & Dave McSherry, cough up a deluxe, remastered expansion of their ’94 debut LP as the 2nd classic offering from Forever Records’ reliquary.

Last on wax in 2002, ‘Old Codes New Chaos’ now returns to circulation as an expanded edition. It all ideally portrays the Humberside duo at an early crest of their powers, dovetailing the UK’s prevailing threads of ambient and deep house, chill-out music, and more whimsical indie, with a signature wit and relative outsider charm that can possibly be attributed to their roots in Hull, where they would be cited as a formative cue for likes of Richie Culver (although you may need to squint your ears to get that). More generally, and with the benefit of hindsight, they can be heard as very symptomatic of ‘90s halcyon days, when a new wave of youth found their dancing feet, and needed a soundtrack to cushion rave comedowns of this type. 

Following on from Forever Records’ PWOG reissue (crafted on the opposite side of the North Sea a few years earlier), ‘Old Codes New Chaos’ shares a similar thing for grooving sensuality and atmospheric levity, but with a pastoral English touch that can’t help but evoke bucolic summers and likely induce huge nostalgia from those there at the time, or likewise in the eternal now. Front to back it’s balmy pleasure to stroll from the siren calling deep house swag of ‘Mermaids’ thru the harmonic glow of ‘New Chaos’, taking in the Weatherall-style swagger of ‘Brazilification’, or K&D type lounge music of ‘The Sheriff’, to the 18 min electro-dub-house collage of ‘Fila Funk.’

items.body:
An extra sugary batch of queer cult pop fancies on Cairo’s ever-wonderful Nashazphone label; super melodic, passionate synth-pop songs about boys, beauty and the melancholy of youth, tipped for fans of Elli et Jacno, Taxi Girl and Mathematiques Modernes.

‘Hélas’ collects 15 songs from the repertoire of Neoboris, an infamous Bordeaux/Pau duo highly active in the late ‘90s and early ‘00s. Drawing on direct Punk, Wave, Rave Culture and “Variété Française” influences, it functions as a perfect time capsule of a very specific era and mood: a boy-and-girl duo celebrating their love for boys, with melancholy and beauty.

"The origin story reads like an archetype, but the details make it sting. One half of Neoboris came out of hardcore raves and Bordeaux punk bands, carrying the raw‑throated urgency of that milieu; the other, Boris, grew up on New Wave and goth, a born songwriter whose melancholic streak ran as deep as his knack for hooks. Together they found a common altar in Elli et Jacno, Taxi Girl, Mathématiques Modernes – that peculiarly French intersection where cheap drum machines, fragile synth lines and deadpan vocals can suddenly break your heart. Out of that devotion came a duo aesthetic: compact songs, simple structures, lyrics that flirt with kitsch and then side‑step into something sharper, all delivered with the kind of chemistry you can’t rehearse into existence.

Their shows were wild in the way that only under‑funded, over‑feeling gigs can be: feedback squeal, rushed tempos, voices occasionally cracking, the two of them radiating that mix of shyness and bravado you get when you’re singing your secrets out loud. Hélas gathers the studio and home‑recorded echoes of that era and orders them into an emotional arc – from rush to comedown, infatuation to regret, celebration to elegy. The production sits right on the fault line between DIY and pop: drum machines slightly out of time, synth presets pushed into unexpected shapes, guitars toggling between brittle and blissed, all wrapped around melodies that would sound just as right on a transistor radio as in a squat.

The shadow that hangs over the record is Boris’s death in 2008, a break so abrupt it turned the entire project into unfinished business. The surviving member’s decision to keep singing these songs “everywhere I can” isn’t nostalgia, it’s a refusal to let that voice vanish into footnote status. Hélas makes that refusal tangible: 15 tracks that re‑situate Neoboris not as local cult trivia but as part of a larger, messy history of queer‑coded, under‑the‑radar French pop. You hear the mourning in the title, of course, but the music itself leans hard into joy – messy, melancholy, shoulder‑to‑shoulder joy, the kind you find on cramped dance floors at four in the morning. Singing with him then, now, and forever: Hélas documents that promise in all its scruffy, luminous detail."

One for the lovers and the ravers.

Key Chicago house architect Ron Trent departs the club for the bedroom under new alias La Marr, a new vent for his most romantic, sublime soundscapes, warmly advised FFO Detroit Escalator Company, Terre Thaemlitz, Wally Badarou, Klaus Schulze, MvO Trio

Light candles/incense and scatter petals for optimal effect when immersing in La Marr’s debut ‘Mood Programs’ EP, which finds a perfect home nestled amid Music From Memory’s precious, timeline-twining cuts of new age ambient, kosmiche, and Balearic wist. It’s also a natural, logical progression from the sort of depths usually secreted in Trent’s albums, but here given full sides to unfurl their functions, which we’re sure will also sound dead tasty, syrupy slow, on 33-not-45. 

He paints the lushest 12 min panorama of elliptical stereo pads, floating organ cloud structures and skin-stroke arps in ‘Good Magic’, edging on similar terrain to Terre Thaemlitz’s golden revision of Tangerine Dream’s ‘Love on a Real Train’, where a fine line of hand played drums emphasises the swaying groove - swooning either bed-ways or a little rug-cut, depending on your disposition - before ‘Clear’ hustles a palette of the slinkiest Afro-Latinate, Brazilian rhythms under big, dusky skies, hinting at Manuel Göttsching via MvO Trio. 

Your ears do not deceive you: this one is proper lush.

'Don't Know How To Change' is Julian Lindsey’s debut EP, released on the Sound of Vast.

"Since Julian Lindsey slid smoothly into the New York House scene back in 2014, he has become renowned for his sharp musical intuition, slick selections and a symbiotic relationship with the crowd. He takes the groove on the record and transmits it to the groove on the dancefloor.

The title track is smooth beyond belief, funky house keys and a laid back soulful vocal work with the bass to make your hips start to move, before a house backbeat takes you by the hand onto the dancefloor. At 3:15 mins, Julian Lindsey plays his ace card with a TB-303 acid tweak drenched with emotion. Just superb. The Subb-an Dubmix stays true to the original, claps and snares bring a dancefloor immediacy, the vocal line chopped to bring the funk. Ibiza will go wild for this Dubmix.

Miami Air starts with a Funktion-1-lovin’ deep velvet groove. Close your eyes and you can almost smell that dusky, warm Atlantic coast beach at sunset, driving with the roof down as the lights start to twinkle across Vice City and the bass drum beats through your fulcrum. A perfect companion for Don’t Know How To Change. Francesca Lombardo’s remix takes Miami Air from dusk to deep night, A mini Moog 4/4, rimshot claps and a vintage synth line guides you past midnight onto the dark, humid dancefloor where bodies writhe.

Julian Lindsey tells us more: The EP is really the story of my relationship with house music and a snapshot of where I was in my life when I made these tracks. I have an obsession with house music that is borderline unhealthy. The sound is rooted in 2010s house music, which is the era where my love for house music really developed."

items.body:
An almost forgotten but bona fide Ambient classic floats up on this edition with the legendary Glasgow-based Ampoule label, newly remastered with a bonus cut for added immersion - highly recommended to fans of BoC, Balil, Porter Ricks.

Still every bit as woozy and gouched-out as we remember, Pub’s gingerly wistful debut album ‘Do You Ever Regret Pantomime?’ is a cult classc for those that know; a sublime example of a peculiar sound at its sensitive best. Back in 2001 it saw lots of rotation at our auld shop Pelicanneck and has since become prized for its effervescent melodies and light-touch drum programming that acknowledged and parsed influence from then-contemporary hip hop and post-rock as much as the prevailing trends of ambient and minimal techno. 

A plangent, elusive sense of nostalgia that arguably prefigures modes of hauntology beautifully percolates the album, dwelling on a melancholy state of mind that, with hindsight, speaks to a timeless sort of wistfulness and tentative tension surrounding the early years of the millennium. The tracks are perhaps detectably burred with a gently rolling accent and crepuscular glow that we’d attribute to Pub’s Scottish provenance and which clearly resonates with BoC, so it’s maybe best to play this album after theirs, when its vaporised textures and thizzing melodic tendrils will best work their exceedingly subtle yet palpable magic. 

The real deal this one.

items.body:
A gorgeous, properly influential ambient drift classic resurfaces complete with a new extended piece evoking gauzy nostalgia for late ‘90s/early ‘00s styles.

The glimmering iridescent dub electronics of’Summer’ bobs up from 2000 in the wake of a reissue for the reclusive Scottish artist’s lush debut album  ‘Do You Ever Regret Pantomime?’ (2001). There’s a legion of people out there for whom this was really one of the most definitive and influential records of the era, originally surfacing via Vertical Form and creating a sort of bridge between the foundational Chain Reaction template and the wave of atmospheric, Detroit-indebted UK Techno typified by the Likemind label, Stasis, Irdial etc. 

Newly remastered to taste, the original stretches out to the horizon with a groove and lilt that feels something like a re-wired take on ‘E2-E4’ overseen by Mark Fell and Terre Thaemlitz. It’s just inarguably lush, uplifting gear.

‘Fragile Root’ is exclusive to this release, and, although we’re not sure if it’s new-new, or old-new; either way it’s a perfect example of Ambient sculpting at its slinky and melancholic best, strongly recalling Plaid’s ‘Anything’ (the best ever Plaid track, right?) as well as the new wave of UK based producers at the time orbiting around labels like DeFocus, Headspace etc. A throwback - but weirdly a strongly comforting one.

items.body:
Finally, for the first time on vinyl, 'Skinned' is Danish producer/singer ML Buch's sparkling debut album. Like her breakthrough 'Suntub', it's a hook-y fusion of OPN-grade electronics, smart, sparse orchestral flourishes and grade A songwriting that nuzzles between Erika De Casier, James Ferraro, Oklou and Tirzah.

Made using almost all MIDI instruments, 'Skinned' is vintage pop record that's been dragged, kicking and screaming into the digital age. Buch is a knowledgeable, literate songwriter and a skilled producer, and if Daniel Lopatin tried to emulate the garbled sound of soft-rock radio, she manages to prize that process open and re-insert the sickly-sweet harmonies and earworms that made those OG songs so enduring. She drills into contemporary problems on 'Touching Screens' - "I'm touching screens more than skin" - but braids her expertly AutoTuned vocal harmonies with quirky pitch-bent canned electronic wails, corny bass twangs and drum rolls that sound as if they've been grabbed from an '80s power pop sample pack. It shouldn't work, but Buch approaches her songs without irony - she's clearly got a deep connection with the pop music she's referencing, from Belinda Carlisle to Fleetwood Mac.

'Can't Get Over You With You' is a little edgier, breaking up the radio pop bass hits and sickly sweet harmonies with Ferraro-esque soundfont play-offs and frazzled, off-grid synth solos, and on 'Sap', she descends into nauseous, reverberant ambience, sounding like a stuck Enya CD. All the idiosyncratic touches that made 'Suntub' such an essential album are present, and although 'Skinned' isn't quite as exquisitely developed, its quirkiness makes it all the more intriguing.

Returning after a decade-long break with none other than Isis/Sumac frontman Aaron Turner at the helm, Neurosis move into a new era with their sickest album since the iconic 'Through Silver in Blood'. Tipped!

It would have been easy to assume that Neurosis would have folded after guitarist and vocalist Scott Kelly, one of the band's founder members, was dismissed following domestic abuse allegations. Indeed, as late as in January last year, it looked like things were fizzling out when drummer Jason Roeder claimed he was ready to sell his music equipment and retire from touring. And it would have made sense, too; Neurosis have been active since the mid-1980s and defined a sound that would evolve into "post-metal", pulling influence from hardcore, prog, industrial music, ambient and sludge and inspiring a legion of followers. They never really lost their mojo, either - even their last album, 2016's Steve Albini-recorded 'Fires Within Fires' was pretty universally regarded as one of that year's best metal releases. But truth be told, they'd started to repeat themselves; locked into Kelly's grim, agonized lyrics, they were starting to sound like their own gloomy tribute act. If it was the end, they'd had a good run.

So 'An Undying Love...' is in many senses a total surprise Not only is the band back, re-energised, but they have a new vocalist and guitarist in tow: Turner, whose old band Isis were arguably the most important members of post-metal's second wave. You might consider the new Neurosis lineup as the ultimate post-metal supergroup, then, and 'An Undying Love...' is the record that proves the credentials of everyone involved. Unlike its tight, almost too brief predecessor, this album is a return to the epic, sprawling songwriting that both Neurosis and Isis perfected at their respective peaks. And it's incredibly expansive, too; anyone who's been following Turner in recent years will already know how open-minded he is, whether it's with his work with Moor Mother and Keiji Haino as Sumac or his various genre-bending collaborations. Here, there's an extra layer to the Neurosis sound that fills out their sludgy, lurching epics with the meticulously engineered haze of Isis's milestone 'Oceanic'.

Where Neurosis's last few albums had been shaped by their long-time collaboration with Albini, this one sounds like a clean break, mixed and recorded by Oakland's Scott Evans, who worked on Turner's Sumac records. It's still Neurosis, with those slow, almost symphonic atmospheres and the unmistakably tight rhythm section, but there's even more going on here, whether it's the unsettlingly effective breakdowns that often replace the band's usual instruments with synths and pounding drum machines, or the stacked feedback loops and scratches that fill their riffs with even more tension. Turner's lyrics, too, offer the band a new dimension to explore. "The separation that burns our hearts / is the root of all our disease," he bellows on the opener 'We Are Torn Wide Open' over radio interference. "We've forgotten how to live so we suffer." Self-referential in their own way at first, they move on as the band does, rolling through themes of environmental collapse, division and redemption. 

It's worth it just for the payoff delivered by the album's side-long finale 'Last Light', shifting from hi-BPM dark gabber into pure symphonic sludge, using its hefty runtime to properly display what this nu-Neurosis (NeurIsis?) is capable of. Really, it's not just the band's most vital record in years, it's one of the best metal albums we've heard in way, way too long.

items.body:
A new set of unreleased sessions from Sun Ra's prolific early 1970s period bundled with two '80s live jams, 'East Two +7' is one for fans of Ra's off-world electronic material - ie. his most vital shit.

Honestly, you'd win us over with the fifteen minute 'East Two' alone. The 15-minute track was recorded in Chicago's Streeterville Studios in 1972 and emerged during a fertile period for Ra, towards the end of his time on New York City's avant-garde circuit. That year he dubbed 'Space is the Place', 'Universe in Blue' and the Moog-augmented sidestep 'Discipline 27-II', and that was only the beginning. Ra and his collaborators spent two days in Streeterville and went deep; Ra played synth, Pat Patrick was on bass, Kwame Hadi played trumpet and John Gilmore handled the tenor horn. And Ra's contribution is subtle at first; he hangs back, playing dissonant, sci-fi tinged tones behind his bandmates' wilder, bendier solos before lurching forward, jamming out nasty organ runs and unhinged oscillations before the track grinds to a halt.

Elsewhere, there's the 1973 track 'In Tomorrow's Realm', where Ra plays against the Arkestra's Ronnie Boykins on bass and an unravelled version of 'Yesterdays' that was recently discovered on an unlabelled reel-to-reel tape, featuring Ra on the Yamaha YC-30 combo organ. Even the two live recordings, a version of the 'Omniverse' favorite 'The Place of Five Points' captured in Columbus, Ohio in 1985 and a 'Fate in a Pleasant Mood' pit dub from the Arkestra's 1984 tour through Egypt and Europe, are worth checking into.

"After a successful run of early EPs and his debut double LP You!, Producer and Singer-Sing Writer Alek Lee returns to Antinote with his new album Like a Flower — an 8-track journey (plus 3 digital bonus dubs) that feels like open-heart surgery. With raw vulnerability, Lee exposes his deepest fears, pain, and inspirations, singing straight from the gut, but also sending words of inspiration and hope.

From dub-infused vibes like the opening track Alright featuring My Lord, to grungy ‘90s trip-hop stylings on Compensation and the title track Like a Flower, the album showcases Alek’s wide emotional and sonic range.

He shifts seamlessly into smoky, Sade-esque moods on tracks like Change, Let the Sun Just Shine, and Hold On — intimate ballads exploring heartbreak and existential reflection.

With his signature blend of melodica, live percussion, guitars, vocal choirs, and lush '80s synths, Alek Lee locks you into his unique sonic universe. His brutally honest, yet deceptively simple lyrics are dressed as balearic dub-pop bangers."

Finally, Kompakt issue a true GAS outlier on vinyl for the first time, recorded in 1989 and containing some of Wolfgang Voigt’s earliest and starkest recycling of magisterial Wagner loops, closest to the ends of The Caretaker, Philip Jeck, Kevin Drumm.

One of those releases that has lurked on our shelves since 2008 as a book and CD, ‘November 89’ exists in the margins of Wolfgang Voigt’s GAS canon as its creepiest and most occluded evocation of long walks in the Bavarian forests. While other GAS classics ooze a sort of dappled warmth breaking thru the trees in their widescreen dub techno strolls, you can fully feel the light dying over the horizon and the forest drawing in on this particularly gloomy, hour-long suite. 

As the title suggests, it was mostly, remarkably, made in ’89, back when Voigt was finding his feet between techno, house and indie-pop, and nearly a decade before he co-founded Kompakt with Michael Mayer & Jürgen Paape - by which time he was a full-fledged rave dynamo as Love Inc. and myriad others notable projects. And, in that sense, it can be heard as his ‘Selected Ambient Works 89-95’ - or perhaps more pertinently with SAW II vibes - in his nascent attempt to chase the ambient dragon, which surely endures for its strangely nostalgic, unheimlich qualities.

An educated guess leads us to think the first three were made in ’89, taking in the nightfall scenery of smudged symphonic strings and icy crackle to ‘Der Wald’, plus the muddied bass waltz and spectral pall of ‘Das Moor’, thru the self-evidently titled centrepiece ‘1989-11-01’, bristling with a digitally iridescent dread. ‘Tal 90’ and ‘Nah Und Fern’, which shares its title with the 2008 boxset, were most likely made a little later, and find the wintry doom thawing to the GAS-eous forms we’ve all come to deeply know and adore. 

A true evergreen for deep ambient techno connoisseurs, no less

items.body:
Returning to Hive Mind, Lebanese artist Yara Asmar collages reel-to-reel recordings of her family in Beirut with surreal cinematic interjections and textures extracted from her arsenal of toy instruments, metallophones and homemade music boxes.

If there's one thing that stood out about Asmar's excellent last Hive Mind offering 'synth waltzes & accordion laments', it was the storytelling. A puppeteer, Asmar's used to arranging her art into narrative segments, and pulls us further into her world on 'everyone i love is sleeping...', cutting her playful Švankmajer-esque chimes and resonances with ferric memories that edge us precariously towards war. Now based in upstate New York, she remembers Beirut not with nostalgia; "there is no future to yearn for and the past does not exist," she explains. It's a story about Asmar's isolated present that tells us who she is, via ghostly echoes and instruments weighed down with cultural baggage.

Asmar acknowledges the implications of using music boxes and toys, complaining that they're "burdened with sentimentality", so it's fascinating to hear her deal with this head on. Unlike her previous albums, that treated the instruments with a level of reverence, there's a purposeful disregard for order here that keeps things interesting. At their most affecting, her soundscapes are built from instruments abused, rather than used; chimes that ring through the album's early tracks distorted until they're sawed resonances on 'of the always puzzle...', and her music boxes sound like a doomed gamelan orchestra on the brief but satisfying 'for now we leave...'.

Asmar leads us through childhood, with twanging languid melodies on 'there are glorious labyrinths...' to genuine memories of home, ending with the resonant 'sounds from home', a set of powdery environmental recordings that she overlays with accordion and dissociated noise.

items.body:
Remastered and returned to vinyl for the first time since 1959, 'Blues in the Mississippi Night' is one of Alan Lomax's most impactful recordings, a historical document of the blues and the Black culture that surrounds it that was so controversial at the time it had to be released under pseudonyms. This new edition arrives with full transcriptions and detailed liner notes.

In 1947, just a few years before he escaped to London during the McCarthy era, Lomax invited legendary bluesmen Big Bill Broonzy, Memphis Slim and Sonny Boy Williamson to perform at the Town Hall in New York City as part of his Midnight Special concert series. He shuttled them over to the nearby Decca Studios and warmed up the machines, asking them not just to perform some of their well-known standards, but to discuss "the blues" - the legacy of the music itself and the realities of Black life in America, warts and all. It's hard to relay just how controversial this was at the time; Black folks knew, but to white America it was an elaborate fiction, a grim Jim Crow-era reality they weren't ready to accept. And when the stories were printed in the Common Ground magazine under the title 'I Got the Blues', they caused so much outcry that the album's release was delayed for a decade. In the interim period, Lomax used snippets of the session for the BBC Radio documentary 'The Art of the Negro. And even when it was eventually pressed by United Artists in 1959, it was attributed to "Natchez, Sib & Leroy", made-up names that protected the identities of the artists themselves, in case of repercussions. 

Listening back now, it's enlightening, putting an often misunderstood American reality into sharp focus. The album is hinged on conversations between two of the artists: Broonzy, an ex-sharecropper who had served in the First World War before picking up guitar on the Chicago circuit and Slim, a bandleader and long-time associate of Broonzy's whose distinctive piano playing defined the era. Proper blues standards, prison songs and chants are woven instinctively into the conversation to contextualize the words and it's incredibly effective; the culture itself should already be telling us the story, but it's even more tangible when we hear the words from two old friends recounting their lived reality. And it's far more valuable to hear this - a primary source - than the rantings of ornery collectors and critics.

Bassbin auteur Martyn’s knack for album craft is clear on his refined yet expansive 5th solo LP, landing 8 years since ‘Voids’ with eight diverse cuts that ideally portray his strength in jazz-rooted diversity, developing binds with a range of distinctive instrumentalists and voices: Duval Timothy, Lucinda Chua, Musa Okwonga among them.

It's an unexpected one - but give it a minute. While the late-album collaboration with tenor sax don Cisneros sounds like a weighty modern jazz flex that could have been snatched from any number of Dusty Groove-cosigned reissues, and the moonlit 'Remnants', featuring Chua on cello and Timothy on piano, sounds as if it's been purpose built for an A24 soundtrack, Martyn's personality shines through when the various threads are knotted together. The D.C.-based Dutchman has admired jazz from a distance for decades and seems to understand its impact on his craft; just check 'Hypnotoxic Laser', a slow, jungle-inspired roller that harks back to the best early Photek gear, or the album's impressive lead single 'Heavy Sound', that imagines what Martyn's taut post-dubstep might sound like if it was played by a jazz quartet. 

His one-on-one collaboration with Timothy, 'No One Plays The Game', is a good opportunity to hear those unmistakably airy harmonies juxtaposed with very different sonics and 'Phantom Jazz' is an impressive diversion too, an update of Skalpel's dimly lit formula with drums from Mischa Porte.

Italian club shapeshifter Piezo pulls from a native history of cosmic disco, trance and electronica on a diverse handful of aces nodding to Beppe Loda, Marco Passarani and Donato Dozzy.

Named for the Tibetan funerary rite, ‘Sky Burial’ follows in a guess-again run of dub, hard drum, and breaks-driven works of the past decade to portray Piezo at full dancefloor wingspan. They’re all fine-tuned for effortless motion, from a sleek title tune that spotlights how synth-pop paved the way for trance - think Chris & Cosey-meets-Pet Shop Boys - thru the urgently uptempo yet elegant electronica of ‘Their Amnesiac Colours’ harking late ‘90s Pssarani via Orbital, and the D’Arcangelo-type braindance of ‘Vimelodica’, next to something like Beppe Loda meets Black Merlin on ‘Bardo Climax’, and echoes of Donato Dozzy’s take on modern Roman trance in ‘Trunks’.

Last seen on vinyl in 1990, Clock DVA’s scuzzy blast of noirish skronk, spangled psych and cold war spy funk for Throbbing Gristle’s Industrial Records remains a wicked relic of a pivotal 1980 and exemplary of Adi Newton’s expansive vision - RIYL James Chance & The Controtions, Suicide, Cabaret Voltaire.

‘White Souls In Black Suits’ was recorded by an early iteration of CDVA led by an Adi Newton who a few years earlier had departed The Future, a prototype of The Human League, and was beginning to embark one of late C.20th electronic music’s most fascinating projects. The eight-part album captures Newton (voice, synth, clarinet, bowed electric guitar, and tape treatment) blaring beside Clock DVA co-founders Steven James Turner, David J. Hammond, Charlie Collins, Roger Quail, and Simon M. Elliott-Kemp, with Cabaret Voltaire’s Steven Mallinder & Richard H. Kirk overseeing from the studio booth at their Western Works Studio. Aye, lad, it’s a proper Sheffield thing, like vinegar buns, cutlery and inclines.

At the fore Adi Newton’s vox channels a troubled soul of late ‘60s garage psych and late ‘70s goth and industrial qualities, comparable to Gen P-O as much as Takashi Mizutani and Peter Murphy, but with his own prowling, scowling swagger binding their songs, stepping from th clipped cold wave funk of ‘Consent’ and fuzzed up sleaze of ‘Discontentment (1 & 2)’, thru 10 mins of lysergic, strung-out psych mumble and caterwaul on ‘Non’. They hit a needling, wiry ace with ‘Relentless’, and sow seeds for CDVA’ oddest tangents and fascinations with “surveillance, obsession, and psychological decay” with the soundscapes of ‘(Film Soundtrack Keyboards Assemble Themselves at Dawn)’ and atonal collage ‘Anti-Chance’.

Japan’s classic knack for slick jazz emulation is in debonaire effect on The Milky Way’s 1979 suite of bossanova and elegant city pop, produced by guitarist Makoto Matsushita and ambient pioneer Yasuaki Shimizu. Last available on LP 10 years ago, now trading for triple figures 2nd hand…

“Wewantsounds is delighted to present the first official reissue of the highly sought-after 1979 classic, Summer-Time Love Song by The Milky Way. Originally released on the Seven Seas label in Japan and produced by the legendary Makoto Matsushita—the visionary behind the cult masterpiece First Light —the album is a premier example of the sophisticated sound that defined the era. Featuring the cream of Japanese musicians, including Yasuaki Shimizu, the record offers a superb mix of AOR, jazz fusion, funk, and bossa nova. Remastered for vinyl by Colorsound Studio, this deluxe reissue features the original artwork, an 8 page booklet with a new introduction by Paul Bowler.”

items.body:
Snapshot of multigenerational free jazz jams by a trio of lauded Far East artists, bringing together Japanese pianist Masahiko Satoh, Korean saxophonist Kang Tae-Hwan and Japanese percussionist Midori Takada.

"Recorded during a memorial concert for the influential critic and producer Soejima Teruto, TON・KLAMI documents a unique meeting between three pioneering artists whose individual careers helped redefine the possibilities of improvised and experimental music across Japan and Korea from the late twentieth century onwards.

Masahiko Satoh is one of the most influential figures in post-war Japanese jazz and experimental music. Across a career spanning more than six decades, he has continually expanded the possibilities of improvisation through work encompassing jazz, contemporary composition, electronic music and interdisciplinary collaboration.Kang Tae-Hwan is a foundational figure in Korean free improvisation and one of the most distinctive saxophonists to emerge from East Asia. His radical approach to breath, tone and extended technique has influenced generations of improvisers internationally. Midori Takada is internationally celebrated for her groundbreaking work as a percussionist and composer. Her recordings and performances have profoundly shaped contemporary understandings of minimalism, rhythm and environmental sound, earning renewed global recognition in recent years.

TON・KLAMI reflects 33-33's ongoing commitment to uncovering overlooked histories within experimental music. Through a catalogue spanning contemporary commissions, archival recordings and cross-cultural

collaborations, the label seeks to create new contexts for significant work that sits beyond conventional genre boundaries. In bringing this recording back into circulation, 33-33 continues its wider exploration of artistic exchange between Japan, Korea and the international avant-garde. A rare document of spontaneous dialogue between pioneering improvisers Masahiko Satoh, Kang Tae-Hwan and Midori Takada, exploring tension, texture and space through cross-cultural experimental sound."

Japanese noise metal punk Viviankrist’s solo debut of 2019 pitches her somewhere between Merzbow and Russell Haswell with a torrent of tart, distorted oddities for Cold Spring.

Originally issued the same year as her Diagonal album, which shares a quota of unruly electronic DNA, ‘Morgenrøde’ pays witness to the singular, radical artist renewing an early alias after decades playing in black metal (Gallhammer), sludge grind (Congential Hell), and dark ambient (Sehnsucht, with Maniac & Andrew Liles) bands. Taking the reins solo, Viviankrist summons a slew of sour sounds, staking out charred power electronics on ‘Silent Soul’,  and no wave synth bin juice in ‘Spring Song’, along with Merzbow-esque beat noise in ‘Spite Spits’ and ‘Pleasure of Confusion’. But the bets bits are reserved to her more explicitly electronic ones, from the curdled arp steeple and decay of ‘Morgenrøede’, thru the Haswellian acid-electro of ‘Cactus’ and a chattering ‘Higher Minded’ that feels like CoH gone analog.

Whew! A who’s who of contemporary aces rework one of 2024’s strongest LPs, with everyone from Anderson Do Paraiso to Fauzia and Kelman Duran exerting canny spins on Nídia & Valentina’s sticks-meets-circuits polyrhythmic jams.

All hewing faithful to the originals, but delineated in compelling mix of club-ready styles, the remixers prove the classy contemporary mutability of ‘Estradas’ by dare-to-differ batida/tarraxho artist Nídia, and her prolific spar, Valentina Magaletti, who is resoundingly acclaimed for work with literally everyone in the modern scene. 

To play faves, DJ Anderson do Paraíso’s gothic baile spin on ‘Andiamo’ is a clear frontrunner, adding his own vox and illuminating bonds between Portuguese-speaking Afro-Latin diaspora, whilst Fauzia also kills with the glute-twang bassline of her ‘Nasty’ version, and Felt label boss Fergus Jones impresses with his dubbed-out slant on Valentina’s drumming in a ‘No Promises Version’.

Safe to say the rest do not let the side down, with Beyoncé producer Kelman Duran reframing ‘Ta A Bater Ya’ as a heady collage of after-the-storm ambient noise and spectral drums, and Rosa Pistola x Freebot proving ideal remixers for the horny sapphic twiss-up ‘Rapido’, and DJ Plead gets right entangled in the additional layers of percussion to his ’Sicilia Version’. Even Sherelle makes a noted progression from primary colour jungle to ruder, textured nuance on wicked 160BPM version of the title tune.

Landmark, evergreen debut by the eternally charming singer-songwriter, ushering bossa into the emerging tropicália sound in ’67, on a round of songs laced with a political bent that would see him and Caetano Veloso locked up by the military regime in ’69...​

"Arriving on the eve of Tropicalismo, the record places Gil’s guitar at the center of rich arrangements by Carlos Monteiro de Souza, Dori Caymmi, and Leonardo Bruno. Blending samba, bossa nova, carnival traditions, and Northeastern Brazilian rhythms, the album explores social, political, and religious themes. The title track “Louvação,” co-written with Torquato Neto, calls for collective awareness, while “A Rua” carries a bittersweet nostalgic tone. Gil’s deep connection to Bahia flows through “Beira-Mar” (with Caetano Veloso), and his poetic imagination shines in “Lunik 9,” reflecting on the space race. “Ensaio Geral” captures the political energy of carnival, while “Rancho da Rosa Encarnada” (with Torquato Neto and Geraldo Vandré) evokes traditional festivities. Highlights include the rhythmically inventive “Roda,” the celebratory “Viramundo” (with Capinan), and the nostalgic “Água de Meninos.” The romantic “Maria (Me Perdoe, Maria)” offers a moment of intimacy, while “Procissão” closes the album with a powerful reflection on faith and society."

Hashman Deejay mints a new alias with a ruck of curdled circuitry, hardcore jungle tekno and downbeats acutely advised FFO Rezzett, Demdike Stare, Jega, Ragga Twins, 2 Bad Mice.

A longtime regular on Future Times and Mood Hut, and also known as half of Aquarian Foundation, Tanner Matt really flexes a ruffer range on Newroomfreak’s eponymous debut. Aside to a pair of gunky beat-less and beatdown works, its all about the full bore rave pressure here, authentically emulating a heyday of ’92-’93 breakbeat hardcore with the brutal body animator ‘Newroomfreak [WIDE]’ calling to mind the Amiga-squashed breaks of early Chaos & Julia Set via Jega’s Skam gems, whereas ’40z’ gets looser, splashier with the breaks in widescreen mode, where his ‘New Out’ wriggles for 10 mins of tail-chasing breaks and flyaway flute licks to get teeth and feet gnashing at the bit.

Maiden vinyl reissue for a cult 1971 slab of cool and vibrant spiritual jazz by flautist Hadley Caliman and pianist Todd Cochran aka Bayeté, who would go on to play keys/synths for Herbie Hancock, Peter Gabriel, Aretha Franklin.

“Wewantsounds continues its reissue program of Bob Shad's cult jazz label, Mainstream Records, with Hadley Caliman's superb 1972 album, Iapetus. Recorded in LA and featuring a heavyweight lineup of West Coast players including Todd Cochran, Woody “Sonship” Theus, Luis Gasca, and Victor Pantoja, the majority of the album was composed by Todd Cochran (aka Bayeté) soon after he had composed Bobby Hutcherson's Blue Note classic, Head On. A true hidden treasure, it is reissued here on vinyl for the first time since 1971, featuring its original gatefold artwork with rare first-generation photos. This edition comes with newly remastered audio and a two-page insert with exclusive liner notes by Todd Cochran, reflecting on Hadley Caliman and the making of the album.”

items.body:
Ernestas Kausylas does scuzzy motorik krautrock, stoner Can-type jams, garage sleaze and widescreen space rock on his 2nd LP with ace Amsterdam label South of North.

‘Lima Echo Crack!’ finds Brokenchord drift farther from electronic moorings into classic, late C.20th guitar, drum and vocal song forms drenched in FX scuzz, as found on his pivotal ‘Stone Island Tracks’. More confident in his combustible drive here, the eight tracks are also not without a hash-head pathos that tempers his mission. 

In ever increasing circles, it turns open out from the motorik propulsion of ‘Prowler’ to 11 mins of full strung-out, lysergic space rock on ‘Liquid Mind Experiment’, dialling it down to a more opiated groove on ‘MKUltra Scarecrow’ and the slackened Neu! 2 B-side styles in ‘CRACK!’ and ‘Get Lost’, before arriving at an expansive mountain-top panorama in ‘PBR’, revving up for the final straits in the dubbed out, grinding ace ‘Tomorrow knows’.

items.body:
Tribal trance techno pioneers PWOG yield a 1st reissue of their debut album since ’93, replete with all tracks from the CD edition on vinyl. RIYL Zoviet*France, Muslimgauze, Mappa Mundi.

A real one for yoghurt weavers and armchair psychonauts, ‘Ov Biospheres And Sacred Grooves’ arrived in ’92 with a broadening and refinement of styles first spied on Psychick Warriors of Gaia’s propulsive, eponymous ’89 entry. Its maiden relaunch now christens Forever Records, a sub-division of Delsin focussed on classic album formats, with an exemplar of early ‘90s ambient techno LP interzones, surely paralleling the UK’s AI movement and characteristic of the way prevailing Euro DIY tape scenes - industrial, ambient, experimental - morphed into techno-trance and house mutations at the cusp of a new decade and era. 

The eight-track LP effectively contains the seeds of trance music as much as modern ambient club in its rangy drive between expansive, linear structures and turns toward downbeat and deep house, all of which were roughly part of the same, strange family during that pivotal period. Of course, the notion of “trance” would be codified, commercialised over the next decade, but in PWOG’s hands the sound is wide open and better defined by its sense of romance and an hypnotic immersion that patently endures for shine-eyed retro-futurists and those able to squint ears, hear the bridges between styles. 

A case in point is ‘The Challenge’, which best resembles their cult debut EP, but with a taut aerodynamic akin early Plastikman in Pt. I, but shores up in far trippier realms on a Pt. II that better reflects the rest of the LP. Between the sloshing tribalist rhythms of ‘Linkage’, the 11 min transition from nocturnal dread to buoyant 107BPM ambient house ‘The Tides (They Turn)’, or ultimate dip into warmest Balearic/Goan waters on ‘The Key (Version)’ and gently febrile ambient closer ‘New Edge Mantra’, they display how industrial, house, and ambient were all on the same page, with the same purpose that would be recognised by likeminded aerobic mystics who can join the dots.

items.body:
Steve Gurley and co.’s deeply inspirational run of ’92-’93 hardcore jungle 12”s as Foul Play, compiled on a deadly doublepack via Bristol-via-Berlin torch carriers, Sneaker Social Club.

‘Origins’ contains some of the greatest music of the early ‘90s, particularly spotlighting the transition from rave’s rugged building blocks into artfully hi-tech dance music during that pivotal period. Sifting gems from both volumes of Foul Play’s early EPs on Oblivion Records - including the all-timers ‘Dubbing You’ and ‘Ricochet’ - plus an early 12” for Moving Shadow, the set documents breakbeat hardcore hitting a creative zenith of hyper-chopped soul, dub and pop samples arranged with staccato stabs, cut-up, shuffling breaks and drum machines, right in the pocket before it was codified as jungle. 

Thanks to the studio ingenuity of Steve Gurley, who cut his teeth on these recordings, the set can also be heard to characterise the development of what is known as the hardcore continuum, as defined in Gurley’s subsequent shift into jungle, proper, and then UKG - the ultimate refinement of hardcore’s 2-step shuffles and sexy swerve. The seeds of enduring styles & patterns to come are sown here, from the fractious rush of ‘Finest Illusion’ through the haunting zinger ‘Dubbing You’, to the needlepoint discipline of ‘Ricochet’ and effortless, toes-off-the-floor skip and parry of ‘Screwface’, to the jump-up jungle blueprint ‘Ragatere’.

Alltimers, the lot of them.

items.body:
Finally following up 2019's cult tribal reconstrucción 'System', Delia Beatriz trades hauntology for rhythmic momentum on 'Potpourri', imagining a parallel timeline where guarachero evolved in conversation with acid house and dub techno, fusing its fundamental tresillo reticulations with caustic 303s, Chain Reaction-style echoes and ferocious psychedelic distortions. RIYL Dengue Dengue Dengue, Verraco, DJ Babatr, Safety Trance, British Murder Boys or Lechuga Zafiro

Beatriz has always balanced her dedication to the dancefloor with higher minded obsessions; even her debut album, 2018's NAAFI-released 'Animus', was a 50/50 split of rhythmic experiments and intoxicating soundscapes. But since combing the distant past on 2022's 'The Long Count' and her own musical autobiography on last year's cumbia rebajada love-letter 'Desaceleradas', the forward-thinking club hybrids that reached their peak on 'System' have taken a back seat. Thankfully, she picks up the trail on 'Potpourri', auditing her technique while simultaneously critiquing the past, present and future of Latin dance music. The conceptual rigor that anchored her last run of releases is intact, but 'Potpourri' is an album for the dancers, first and foremost, an arsenal of rave weapons that conspicuously straddles a conflicted border. Even the cover, surreptitiously shot on the bridge between the USA and Mexico, reflects the album's provenance, its grafting of genetic material sourced from Detroit, Chicago, Mexico City and Monterray.

'System' was an attempt to blend tribal guarachero with industrial techno and 'Potpourri' focuses the concept further, burying its roots deeper in techno's subsoil. Over an album length this time, Delia considers the fast-paced, non-linear way tribal legend Javier Estrada worked to redevelop her approach to writing club music from the ground up. "It's a manifesto for rethinking form and sound in dance music," she explains. "By stepping outside traditional structures and embracing the potpourri approach, I'm creating new meaning with familiar rhythms." We can hear exactly what that means on the cheekily-titled 'Assimilate', when familiar syncopated thuds plunge through a heaving mass of 303s, forming a compound that's part Jeff Mills, part Chico Sonido. But it's that high end that has us properly gripped; Beatriz knows that it ain't just kicks that'll infuse her potpourri so peppers in aromatic tresillo shakers, cutting almost to silence at the track's halfway point to make sure we fully comprehend the pyramid.

Similarly, on '2placesatonce', her corrupted hoover sounds and square wave bleeps are neatly offset with bass tangs and woody acoustic percussion, everything cooked in a layer of grizzled distortion. It helps, no doubt, that the album was mixed by Berlin-based club alchemist Ziúr, who waves her magic wand over the material and gives it the punch it needs to really dominate, whether it's on headphones or belting out of a full Function One setup. And that's completely necessary; just as 'Desaceleradas' was concerned with the feeling of nostalgia evoked from certain phrases or tonalities lifted from cumbia rebejada, 'Potpourri' is driven by the energy that runs through classic club records from both sides of the border. It's music that needs to be experienced on a physical level, inspired by potent memories and powered by Beatriz's desire to keep the contemporary scene evolving or, at the very least, searching.

Sylvain Chauveau's first album since 2022's 'L'effet rebond', 'The Complexity of the Simple' is inspired by a Zen garden, a set of lovingly handcrafted minimal instrumentals that took 10 years to properly shape.

Chauveau was marveling at the lines drawn in the gravel of Kyoto's Tokaian temple when the idea for 'The Complexity of the Simple' appeared. He's been refining (and reducing) his sound for decades now - his last set was called 'Ultra-minimal' - but there's a different level of focus on display here, something controlled and, if not emotionless, then at least contemplative. By stripping away the fat of romance and aesthetic grandstanding from his earlier material, Chauveau has found a niche that's as peaceful and philosophically absorbing as that Zen garden. And, considering a future without fossil fuels and the producing, playing and listening that new era might provoke, he engages in a push and pull with sound that's engaging without being mawkish.

'Le Zen Dans L'Art Du Tir À L'Arc' transports us to Kyoto with its measured rhythmelodic chimes - from handpan, glockenspiel and synth - and on 'The Guitar Piece I Wrote for Masumi', Chauveau plays his instrument so softly that it almost evaporates. On 'Wabi Sabi for Beginners', he layers warbling synth tones on top of each other, creating beating rhythms that only appear if you're really tuning in, and on the final track 'Lignes Tranquilles Dans Le Gravier Blanc', he's joined by Tetuzi Akiyama on acoustic guitar and his longtime spar Cyril Secq, who follow his lead, playing lowercase notes into tempered radio interference and subtle, almost imperceptible environmental recordings.

items.body:
Sickest Dagbani dance-pop from northern Ghana, all produced by Mohamed “Ebony” Fuseini of Studio Simpa, and voiced by Dickson Gawani, Bala Zaaku, and Yaa Naara, among others - FFO DJ Tobzy, DJ Diaki, Nozinja, Music From Saharan WhatsApp

Issued on the Autotune The World label that shares its name with Chris Kirkley's long-running NTS show, ‘Digital Dance Music on VCD from Dagbon, Northern Ghana’ follows the show and label’s hyper-specific focus on the likes of Tecnobrega from Brasil and Caribbean Soca & Chutney with a rare jag upcountry in Ghana’s predominantly Muslim north. 

Armed with phone mic, FL Studio, and the best local singers on speed dial, Mohamed “Ebony” Fuseini updates local styles of Dagbani dance rhythm and melody with shiny VSTs and, of course, nuff autotune, to bring the rural sound closer to those from bigger cities, as heard on shared mp3s and physical media such as VCDs.

Available and traded at local markets, but rarely heard by international ears, those VCDs feature footage of women shaking hips - a “light cultural transgression” in the mostly Muslim area - with lyrics by local “Gawani”, flashy singers such as Dickson Gawani, Bala Zaaku, and Yaa Naara, with something to show, and matched by the energy of Ebony’s productions. Not as rushy as, say DJ Tobzy from Lagos, or DJ Diaki in Mali, Ebony’s Studio Simpa cuts are more melodic, pop-wise, maybe best compared with the colourful hi-energy of Shangaan Electro, heard on highlights from Dickson Gawani’s acidic percolator ‘So Tinha’ (also in a killer 12” bonus mix!), thru the lilting ballad ‘Baamunu’ by Obaako, to the unique skank of Aminu Dakogu, and the supremely light-headed effect of ‘M Be Adama’ by Alhassan Kukuonaa - all primed to light a fire on summer ’26 ‘floors.

items.body:
Following June's brilliant 'Rhythm Archives', Holy Tongue's Al Wootton continues his hot streak, landing on Sähkö with half an hour of hazed, immersive rhythmic experiments, tracking from vintage dub(step) to minimal techno and confidently striding thru percussive forms that echo from the Balkans to North Africa. RIYL Shackleton, Azu Tiwaline, Muslimgauze, T++, Deena Abdelwahed.

Ever since he dispatched with the Deadboy moniker a few years back and reached into dubbier, more percussive spaces, Wootton's been figuring out exactly where his dexterous productions fit in.He's been most at home on his own Trule imprint, operating at his own pace and shaping the aesthetics as he goes, and 'Rhythm Archives' felt like a mark in the sand, a record that matched his interest in vintage gear and classic production methods with his dedication to wide-eyed, punkish experimentation. 'CRUX', his first record for legendary Finnish label Sähkö, follows that lead, assembling four long percussive jams that sound as if they've toppled off the timeline - if someone told us it was material rescued from a forgotten reel-to-reel, we'd believe it.

There's an outline of dubstep visible in the background on opener 'Essene' that's enhanced by the Skull Disco-esque sub-undulations and wormhole-splitting tape echoes, but the hollow hand drum runs and hallucinatory effects shuttle the composition into darker, more reflective landscapes. Similarly, the busted drum machine intro of 'Per Incanto' might reference Sähkö royalty Mika Vainio and Hertsi, but the track veers leftwards, muddling the mix with psychedelic African Head Charge-style reverberations and trapped, timestretched string loops. It's gear that's intended for deep, intentional listening; the tracks don't contain too much melodic content by design - Wootton's rhythms are layered and hypnotic, and anything else is there to reinforce the general spirit.

Just check 'Cloister', the EP's low-key stand-out, where the lead line is literally just tuned feedback, placed to disorient even the most abstinent listener, or 'Armen', that distorts its sputtering Bruce Haack-in-dub atmosphere with ghosted groans and faint remnants of a trip-hop undercurrent that never fully reached optimal pressure. If you've ingested all the psilocybin from Shackleton's recent run, this is yr next drop.

items.body:
The craziest label in Detroit back with another genius, unfathomable dose of destroyed Techno x Trip Metal, caked in Motor City crud and located on the factory line somewhere between Urban Tribe, H-Fusion and Wolf Eyes​

Seven years on from his debut ‘Bloodsport’, secretive 313 artist K-6000 only jags deeper into Detroit’s scuzzy underbelly on the rough hewn rhythmic noise and atmospheric trip metal of ‘War Games’. The 6-part album surely evokes the dystopia of modern Detroit’s knackered architecture in its cranky tone and offbeat structure, but also signals the underlying soul of its entities, and the lost futures they live thru, in its textured play of psyched sax and guitar spectres meshed with sampledelic tapestry of disembodied voices. 

A record that leaves dirt under yr nails, it unfurls at its own steady pace from free jazz noise like some Wolf Eyes re-score of Robocop, into grouchy bouts of squashed beatdown psych with ruggedest drum programming comparable to KDJ, Shake and Sherard Ingram’s chops with Kemetrix on the Urban Tribe album. It descends into the sleaziest mire of Blind Pig biker bar blooz, like Captain Beefheart jamming with H-Fusion, around the mid-section, and ultimately buckles into PCP-spiked industrial funk sludge in the final stages. 

Manna for sci-fi free jazz trip metal beatdown hounds, then!

items.body:
Oh man, quite possibly the oddest, cutest thing we’ve heard this year - cult Japanese underground duo Tenniscoats sing and play over a bunch of iconic hip-hop and r'n'b instrumentals on an hour-long tape for A Colourful Storm’s choice Fleetway Tapes sublabel; a concept that’s so brilliantly wtf that we were sold before they even droped a beat.

Saya and Takashi Ueno have never confined themselves to a single genre over the years, bending softer-than-soft whimsical folk, indie pop and psych rock into their own unique shapes - but we still could never have imagined them produce anything like this. We can't tell you how Moopie managed to convince them to yank it from the archives, but it's a total joy - the most eccentric record in Tenniscoats' already distinctive catalogue. 

There's a level of warm fuzz that emphasises the mix was beamed in from another decade - the tape crackles to life with melodica wails that hang remarkably well over the sturdy, bass-heavy instrumental from Mobb Deep's 'Quiet Storm', the lead single from the foundational duo's misunderstood fourth album 'Murda Muzik'. It isn't an obvious track ('Temperature's Rising' or 'Shook Ones, Pt. II' would have been the casual's choice), but it's a stone-cold killer, boasting some of Havoc's dirtiest bass and a snare that could cut glass. Saya does her best to ad-lib her own rap at first, eventually settling into a sort of soft-hued spoken word that floats Havoc's beat from the Queensbridge projects all the way to Tokyo. 

Their take on TLC's 'No Scrubs' is even weirder, with Saya's fragile vocal turn and Takashi's fittingly flamenco-inspired acoustic guitar pushing the overfamiliar beat gently into new territory. You could say 'Hip Hop Tennis' is a karaoke mixtape of sorts, the kind of selection of hastily-made reworks and versions that used to litter the streets outside Brooklyn's Broadway Junction or down on the Lower East Side before the coffeeshops and Cronut stores moved in. But Saya and Takashi's impromptu jams elevate this into the sublime, as if they'd put together a mix of East Coast favourites in the early '00s and spontaneously added their own ingredients on top. Just check the duo's dubbed-out rhymes over Brand Nubian's 'Word Is Bond' or Saya's loungey turn on the underrated Neptunes-produced banger 'Light Your Ass on Fire' and you’ll know exactly what we’re saying.

It's a session that's brimming with a palpable affection for its influences; the first side ends with a lengthy half-speed Nuyorican love-in, and then the second bursts open with an uncharacteristically nursery rhyme-like flip of The Inc's low-key Ashanti-starrer 'No One Does It Better'. Saya's blustery, saturated wails even transform Eve's enduringly popular Dre-produced 'Let Me Blow Ya Mind', while Takeshi attempts to sand down the edges of DMX's 'X Gon' Give It To Ya'. But the best moment comes when Takeshi plays in a minor key over Jeru the Damaja's 'Come Clean' - probably the best East Coast hip-hop track of the '90s - completely re-contextualising it, and trust when we say we thought we'd heard every which way that track could be flipped. 

Even if you've been following Tenniscoats since 2000's 'The Theme of Tenniscoats' - you ain't ever heard them like this.
