Ezekiel Honig's glitchy, concréte house breakout, that originally surfaced nearly two decades ago, finally gets a new lease of life (and a fresh mastering job) thanks to the Keplar imprint.

Back in 2008, the world was already over microhouse. The glitchy, short-lived micro-genre had burned bright for a short moment; Philip Sherburne had coined the term in 2001 and by the time Akufen's 'My Way' had emerged just a year later it felt as if the shine had gone. Honig's 'Surfaces of a Broken Marching Band' arrived in 2008 and sounded like reformed traces of the recent past. The backbone was 4/4, crawling towards a slinky 120BPM minimal house, but the emotional content was completely different. This wasn't material that was aimed at the club or even the afterparty, it was loose, faded gear that Honig had made from meticulously collected foley sounds and environmental recordings - domestic elements that Matthew Herbert would be proud of.

And because the music slipped quietly into its own nook, it still sounds unique now, a record that deserves to be filed alongside Farben's early 12"s and Kit Clayton's iconic 'Nek Sanalet', even Ricardo Villalobos's primo gear - just peep the title track and tell us it doesn't sound like 'Easy Lee' made with a broken shortwave radio and a pinball table. Needless to say, if you're into Mark Templeton (who incidentally appears twice on this record) or the soon-to-be-hauntological Y2K aesthetic, you'll need to grab it without delay.

items.body:
In spring 2025, Abul Mogard and Rafael Anton Irisarri created the source material for their second album, Where Light Pauses in the Silence of the Sun, during a three-day residency at Morphine Raum in Berlin.

"Functioning as both recording studio and performance venue, the space has no stage, with the audience gathered around the performers. Working within an open framework, the duo reshaped the music each evening while recording the performances live to multitrack. Rotary speakers, modular synthesizers and bowed guitar formed the core of their sonic language, captured through a 1970s mixing console and microphones placed around the room.

Back in Mogard’s studio in Rome, the material was further crafted as motifs were stretched, fragments isolated, and tempos dissolved. Irisarri recorded additional guitar textures and treatments in New York, while passages recorded by Martina Bertoni and Andrea Burelli in Berlin reinforced the harmonic centres and brought breath, refinement and a new sensibility to their compositions. The process continued as Mogard’s layering and subtraction reassembled everyone’s parts into the final arrangement.

The album opens with “In the Eastern Wild,” building from a sparse outline into a monumental formation of low-frequency weight, its internal motion shaped by the rotating Leslie speaker. “Over the Domes” widens into a broader acoustic field, where sustained modular tones meet waves of softly plucked guitar. The music then turns inward with “A Blue Descent,” centred on Bertoni’s cello, whose growling timbre introduces a melancholic depth.

At the album’s centre, “In a Quiet Radiance” unfolds around a slow guitar ostinato, its luminous stillness opening into a more expansive and reflective state. Across its ten-minute span, Burelli’s violin lines and Bertoni’s lower cello phrases gradually surface, weaving through the harmonic field. Mogard brings Burelli’s processed voice to the fore, its emotive, operatic presence becoming one of the record’s pivotal moments. “Of Blessed Ages” suspends the sonic flow, shifting between parallel major and minor chords as lingering, slowly decaying melodies shape the music’s internal drift. The closing “Among Shadows” settles into a darker resonance as layered textures recede.

Mogard and Irisarri’s shared language balances restraint and maximalism. UK magazine Crack describes the music as “a tidal wave held in suspension,” while Dutch newspaper de Volkskrant writes, “What a colossal sound, and how this music strikes at the emotions.” Reflecting on the residency sessions, Irisarri recalls: “At moments I genuinely couldn’t tell if a sound was coming from me or from Abul. It stopped feeling like two people making decisions and began to feel like we were inside a system moving on its own."

Marja de Sanctis’ cover artwork revisits the vessel sculpture from the duo’s first album, Impossibly Distant, Impossibly Close. There it appeared as raw, unfired clay. Here it has been fired in the kiln and finished with a glaze. Light gathers on its polished surface and spills into the surrounding space. As she explains, “I wanted to convey the idea of continuity within the duo, and the vessel became a kind of container for that idea. However, their music felt different this time, and with the collaboration of Martina and Andrea, I felt it should have a sleeker, softer, more glamorous look, very distant from the first raw appearance.” The transformation of the vessel from raw clay to fired form suggests a passage from immediacy toward permanence, mirroring the music’s gradual expansion."

items.body:
New from Gi Gi on Mood Hut - dubwise sampledelia​, written between Texas and Australia.

"Gi Gi describes his process as “dubwise sampledelia.” It begins with fragments and ends somewhere else entirely, destabilizing its source material until it stops pointing backward. A borrowed sound, looped and bent, eventually forgets where it came from; it stops referencing anything but itself.

This liquid sensibility shaped his earlier work, music that hovered between drift and propulsion, suggesting the dance floor without fully stepping onto it. Presence was implied, edges stayed soft. The center was always there, but diffused like mist on a screen.

With In Lieu, that center comes into focus. Half written in Texas, half in Australia, the shift isn’t simply geographic, but internal. The record moves with a coiled, anticipatory energy; the drums arrive with more force and the bass organizes the room instead of melting into it. It's dense with the feeling of more bodies in the frame. Textures still smear and refract, but they move around a clearer axis. 

Where past records circled their core, these inhabit it, pulling closer to the body. “Some Of” and “Arque” lean into low-end pressure without abandoning his instinct for drift. "Pink Dirt" circles around mechanical drums and dizzying vocal chops, head-down and visceral.  Elsewhere, voices gain newfound contour, materializing in “Downswept” with intimate musings and nearly forming a lead vocal on the title track before dissolving again.

In Lieu moves with a newfound confidence, compressing inward, sounding closer to the source of its own pulse."

A wealth of DIY dubplates and 45s from Jah Massagan’s East London sound crop up for first time on tape with cherry-picking label Death Is Not The End - heavy roots dub troubles cut at the studios of King Tubby, Lee Perry, Channel One, and Joe Gibbs…

Eljay Mass, son of Jah Massagan’s owner-operator, Lloyd Mass, dips into his dad’s enviable archive for an hour of rare, one-away platters that hail a self-organising rhizome of sound systems which sprang up in the UK with arrival of the Windrush generation, and brilliantly altered the course of music on this strange island in the process. 

The cassette-only session speaks to prevailing links between Caribbean culture and UK inner cities which reverberated from the ‘70s into the ‘80s, and has endured as a touchstone for some of our isles’ most vital music, setting templates for independent distribution networks and producing waves of innovative hybridisation.

Owner-operator Lloyd Mass and his childhood pal and amp builder Tony Mass were a small but steadfast part of preserving these sounds, holding down their Leyton corner of London, where they would pass the torch to Eljay Mass and an extant network of rigs, engineers, Deejays and ravers who really do it for the culture.

Co-produced by Nosaj Thing and 'Donnie Darko' OST guy Michael Andrews, Eartheater's latest is the polar opposite of 2023's 'Powders', ditching the drug and club references and leaning into baby-on-board playlist fodder, including an Oklou feature. RIYL Dido, Dubstar, Sneaker Pimps.

It's still obviously an Eartheater record, more 'Phoenix' than 'Powders'. The album starts strong, with her robotically treated voice sounding oddly soothing next to a full orchestra on 'Eyes of a Dove'. Even the glossy, sync-ready 'Paradise Rains', the album's first single that details her buying back her childhood farm and conceiving her baby, is chewably eccentric, still bound to the same logic that made her bonkers early material so addictive.

items.body:
London-based Malaysian-Australian composer and professor Silvia Lim prioritises close listening on 'Flare', writing quiet, minimal patterns that draw attention to unusual textures and bewitching dissonances.

Having bounced between Malaysia, Australia and the UK growing up, Lim is fascinated by the idea of instability and how that might be represented sonically. She explores a certain kind of fragility on 'Flare', working with the flimsiness of timbre by zooming in to capture the most incidental sounds - the scraping of a slowly pulled bow on the strings or the softness of air blown through a bass clarinet's reed. On the two-part composition 'Grafting', Lim folds in unexpectedly beautiful melodies, letting them grind to a halt completely, or disappear into faint traces beneath resonant ghost notes and stifled wails. There's a trace of folk music in there, buried in the undergrowth. 

And on the four-part 'Field of Play', Lim prepares her instruments with a single tool each time: a hair clip, a bobby pin and piece of cork, presenting the pieces as proof of what sonic shifts these seemingly light preparations might cause. On 'contact', the bobby pin disintegrates the instrumentation, turning the strings into lightly boiling, echoing resonances and on 'hidden place', it's even more disorienting, sounding as if the cello is being lowered slowly into a vast metallic chamber.

items.body:
5 Gate Temple’s high priest John T. Gast turns in 13 mystic trodders and pulse meditations on his first album, proper, dedicated to this style since 2019. Proper fantasy free party x soundsystem tekkerz, for transcendent club pressure.

As torch carrier of a mutant ’90s rave spirit since the early 2010’s, John T. Gast has opened up the cruddiest wormhole between formative Cornish raves and community centre dances. On ‘Infant’ he goes head down, feet first in a particularly briny, rinsed-out style of steppers livicating the enduring geists of early AFX and turbo-charged Jah Shaka with X-amount of moist noise and mystery in the air - the sort of stuff that feels like coming up at the blue hour in a smoke-choked warehouse or damp UK field, mud up to your shins, and loving it.

While it’s his first album since ‘SINEAD MEMORY TAPE’ in ’23, ‘Infant’ is his most substantial salvo in this signature steppers style since at least ‘5GTOUR’ (2019), or even ‘INNA BABALON’ (2016). Satisfyingly crusted with distortion around the edges and fully marshy underfoot, it best portrays the JTG essence in long form, conjuring an hour of heavily hypnotic atmospheres and fritzed production styles practically incomparable to anyone beyond his immediate family of 5GT label oddballs: Tribe of Colin, Xterea, YL Hooi, et al.

Hewing tighter than ever to his thing, JTG generates one of the baddest tools in his bag between the cloven-hoofed whirligig ‘7thfloor (Myrda Mix)’ and the air-stepping gait of ‘Population’, taking in his stride a sort of Kongo Tekno hunch on ‘Going In’ and byzantine ambience of ‘Mrzy 2 (Stone Mix)’,  making room for strains of zoned-out dankness before reeling back to the blunted ends of Caustic Window and the ribboning melodica and jabbing subs of ‘Rising’, before the astro junkyard pound of the title tune and the body-levitating mastery of ‘Goin In (Mer Mix)’.

It all leaves a peculiar tang.

items.body:
Helado Tropical, the debut collaborative album from Helado Negro and Reyna Tropical.

"It didn’t begin with a plan so much as a meeting: two artists orbiting similar questions around language, identity, and music, finally landing in the same room. What followed was less a traditional writing process than a shared unfolding – an instinctive, immersive exchange that stretched across geographies, time zones, and states of being.

The duo first met in June 2024 in North Carolina, brought together by a mutual friend and a loose invitation to spend time in the studio. What might have been a brief session turned into something closer to a three-day sleepover – equal parts conversation, curiosity, and creative risk. Reyna Tropical, accustomed to close-knit collaborations, stepped into new creative territory, while Helado Negro brought a similar sense of curiosity and fluidity.

What emerged was immediate, rather than easing into collaboration, the two found themselves propelled forward by it – building songs in real time, responding to each other’s instincts without over-explaining them. There was no rigid division of roles. One would begin an idea, the other would answer. A melody would suggest a rhythm; a rhythm would reshape a lyric.

Across Helado Tropical, there is a noticeable absence of constraint: not just musically, but conceptually. Both artists share a long-standing resistance to the expectations often placed on Latin music: what it should sound like, how it should feel, what stories it should tell. As they do individually, these two artists create space for something more fluid and personal on this project.

What makes Helado Tropical particularly resonant is the sense of trust that underpins it. Trust in each other, of course, but also trust in instinct and in the process. Much of the album was written through improvisation, with meaning revealing itself only later, as the artists listened back and reflected."

items.body:
A leading light of neo-ambient takes their maiden bow on Glasgow’s stealthily expansive co:clear label after cherished turns with the sferic and Stroom labels.

The International Billionaire’s Love Child, or tiblsc for brevity, is the avatar of a Leipzig-based artist in possession of a distinctive, world-building ambient purview that has clearly stroked a nerve for listeners chasing the modern ambient zeitgeist, especially their couplet of ‘Delusive Tongue Shifts - Situation Based Compositions’ (2021) + ‘Hypertranslucent’ (2022). Those albums’ careful bends of pulpy sentiment and intricate, immersively dreamlike architecture is now echoed in ‘City of Something’, where her tender feel for compression and blends of HD and lo-fi tones fosters a gauzy sense of depth perception and sonorous emotional resonance. 

More so than her previous work, the eight tracks here are laced with a flickering pop spirit that riddles the album’s finely meshed dimensions, calling to mind aspects of Perila that are whisked to its most elegant frisson in ‘Resting Bitch Face’, or catching breathy contrails of an airspun pop song in ‘The Sun Really Is Something Round’, whilst tickling private parts of the imagination with the compressed artefacts of ‘You Just Want’, edging on Shinetiac’s take on smudged sheogaze trip hop in ‘Scare Me’, and teasing the most elusive urges on a secretive, quietly restive closer ‘Until the End of Time’.

In their sublime duo debut the simpatico synth & guitar of Jonny Nash & Tomo Katsurada is seduces to blissed, wind-whispering soundscapes, hashed out over the course of 12 months since Katsurada lent strings to Nash’s ‘Once Was Our Forever’. Dream material FFO Yuta Matsumura, Tenniscoats, Durutti Column...

"Netherlands-based artists Tomo Katsurada (Ex-Kikagaku Moyo / Future Days Radio) and Jonny Nash (Melody As Truth) combine forces for an exploration into the sonic potential of the guitar duo, rooted in their experiences performing together over the last 12 months.

Friends and admirers of each other’s work for a decade, their musical collaboration began in 2024 with Katsurada asking Nash to contribute guitar to his debut EP ‘Dream Of The Egg’. Sensing the need to explore this further, they spent the following year performing together in different configurations, with Nash joining Katsurada’s trio and Katsurada in turn playing with Nash as a duo, across a wide spectrum of spaces, from churches and temples to concert halls, theatres and outdoor festivals. With new ideas developing organically out of these performances, recording new material became the next logical step. A short period of three days was set aside with a clear goal: to capture the essence of their fluid, intertwining melodies and guitar playing in a way that felt as direct and unfiltered as possible. Working from a handful of pre-existing sketches, they left ample room for experimentation to unfold within the process.

The results are presented on ‘At The Emerald Pool’, a collection of ten pieces that offer the listener a full immersion into the pair’s sound. With guitar as the primary instrument for both artists, it is no surprise that the core of the album lies here, specifically in the fluid interplay between the two players. Layers of gentle, delay-soaked fingerpicking often make it almost impossible to distinguish where one player ends and the other begins. As soloists, both Katsurada and Nash have a gift for crafting melodic lines that feel open and ascending, expressive and hopeful without becoming saccharine. Longer, more abstract pieces are counterbalanced by a series of shorter songs, with five vocal tracks appearing across the album. The decision to share vocal duties lends the record a unique quality and a strong sense of variation, bringing a wide expressive range out of a deliberately focused musical framework.

‘At The Emerald Pool’ represents the first chapter in an ongoing musical dialogue, an attempt to capture a moment of connection, openness and discovery, laying the foundation for what continues to unfold."

items.body:
One of the most distinctive and legendary vocal/dub albums of all time, recorded in 1981 by the “dub dentist” Keith Hudson, ‘Playing It Cool & Playing It Right’ is now back in circulation for the first time in over 20 years, when it was first given overdue flowers via Basic Channel And Honest Jon’s ‘Basic Replay’ programme. It still burns with a rare energy, making it an untouchable, foundational text for the ages.

Keith Hudson (1946-1984) was one of dub reggae’s most distinctive innovators, renowned for a run of classic solo albums and productions for U-Roy, Big Youth, Ken Boothe and Horace Andy between 1972 and his untimely passing in 1984. However, Hudson's late period is where the real imperial juice can be found, a time that saw him move from Jamaican to London and New York studios, applying his unfathomable production style to a heavily americanised strain of vocal Soul. ‘Playing It Cool & Playing It Right’ is the pinnacle of that late period, an album that builds layer upon layer of alchemical brilliance.

Hudson’s combination of hooks and complex, highly unusual production is really unlike anything else from the period, or since, crooning in a soul mode made more haunting by a discreetly judicious application of tape FX, endlessly heavy subs, and mixing desk tricks deployed to delirious, almost psycho-acoustic effect.  The album was originally meant to feature one of Hudson's teenage sons to voice the dubs, but in the event the Love Joys, Wayne Jarrett, and inimitably Hudson himself featured at the microphone, with the dozen cuts co-produced by Wackies founder Lloyd ‘Bullwackie’ Barnes - the only collaboration between the two producers. It was originally issued on Hudson’s own label, Joint International, with subsequent pressings on Basic Replay in 2003, making it increasingly sought-after in the years since. 

Alongside reggae’s first concept album, ‘Flesh of My Skin, Blood of My Blood’, ‘Playing It Cool’ remains one the genre’s most important and unusual releases, picking up new disciples with every new wave of listeners taken aback by its stark, brooding blooze and brittle, spectral rendering.

items.body:
The Sultans of Sludge slang a definitive label debut for Sub Pop, bringing their singular sound to roost on a legendary label local to their origins in the US north west, whose rugged landscapes fed directly into the LP’s formidably primal concentration of dualistic energies

Hailing some 30 years since Sunn O)))’s formation, their eponymous 10th studio album reckons with forces of nature - time and space, dark and light - for 80 minutes of air-shuddering pressure limning epic, craggy vistas from a thick haar of distortion. Subtly enlivened with field recordings made in forests near Bear Creek Studios, Woodinville, Washington, where O’Malley says they would “go hiking and be out in the woods, spend time outdoors”, the resulting six-part sequence sees the duo drill down to fundamentals with an absorbing sense of purpose and telepathically-attuned intuition. A notable dearth of other contributors also means it’s one of their truest statements as a duo; just Stephen O’Malley & Greg Anderson howling into the wilds on all instrumentation, from trusted axes to keys and electro-acoustic sorcery. 

At this point, not to labour the arboreal metaphors, but it may take a certified guide to see the wood for the trees in Sunn O))) lands, such is the uniquely coherent sprawl of their sound at 30 years up to the hilt in atonal rock doom. Our hair’s not long enough to lay claim as spirit guides, but after 23 years of bearing witness to them live, and ingesting most of their LPs, we can say this side is wholly emblematic of their radical steez. Between the two 18 minute totems of a ‘XXANN’ laced with location recording of running water at tender points, and a ‘Mindrolling’ monstered with claw-handed riffs, they take it to typically stare-down levels of intensity with the sustained threat of ‘Does Anyone Hear Like Venom?’, and billowing sheets of subharmonic distortion harnessed in ‘Everett Moses’. Closer ‘Glory Black’ is, however, a sort of sore thumb with a relatively conventional riff progression and rising banks of silvery wheeze that collapse into keys and field recordings, hearkening most closely to the duo’s precedents and NW peers in the Sub Pop roster, Earth, or even another touchstone, Black Sabbath, at their most strung out. 

Heavy as your life.

items.body:
Produced by Neek and Jabu's Amos Childs (aka O$VMV$M), Manonmars' third album is syrupy suite of smoke-hazed recollections and free associated reflections set to decelerated bumps, sluggish samples and cloudy drones = sturdy biz FFO Young Echo, Massive Attack, Cold Light, Ka, MIKE, King Vision Ultra, Coby Sey.

Manonmars' 2018 debut is one of those albums we still go back to periodically. It's that rare meeting of minds: a space for O$VMV$M to flex their production muscle and a scratchpad for London-based MC, painter and photographer Jack Martyn Richardson to sketch out a distinct vision of England. And His experiences and impressions on 'Entertainment System' still feel chewable. "Goddess on my arm and both our phones got no service," he quips on 'Goddess'. "Acid is lysergic, psychedelic rock is Turkish." His rhymes aren't throwaway, they map out an underground that's very recognisable, shadowed by O$VMV$M's tuff, effective soundscapes - beats that reference trip-hop, ambient music, exotica and '70s movie soundtracks as much as they do US rap. 

On opener 'Flam3throw3r', Mars raps in double-time over shrill horns that blot out any trace of a beat; Neek and Childs sound as if they relish the negative space, adding chic sword swipes to a track that's got little else to do with the Wu Tang Clan. When a lumbering beat kicks in on 'Decathlon', flipping from downtempo to no-tempo in the final act, it sounds as if it's just there to assert O$VMV$M's commitment to slowness - Mars doesn't even seem to notice, rhyming casually but never losing his flow.

Bristol mainstays Franco Franco and Dali de Saint Paul turn up to assist on 'Volcanic Shield', one of the album's most conventional bangers, led by O$VMV$M's skittering Surf Gang-like beats and morse code blips, and cold light's Birthmark lends his voice to 'Infinite', going bar for bar with Mars over Neek and Childs' slackened funk, blaring out like an old tape on a busted in-car audio system. 'Firewater' takes the same approach, leaving Mars to do his best as snares splash across the spectrum with added sax from Brum-based sound artist Lorenzo Prati. "My bitch white, she can scuba dive and ice climb," he spits. "Put the drink down, I wasn't in my right mind." 

It's music that laughs through the tears - what could be more British than that?

Cold Spring re-issue 'With Extreme Prejudice' by industrial pioneers Sutcliffe Jugend (ex WHITEHOUSE).

"Harsh extreme electronic pioneers Sutcliffe Jugend return with an album of all new material. Three years in the making, and with numerous reworkings, "With Extreme Prejudice" finds Sutcliffe Jugend at the top of their game. Forcing the listener to question their own prejudices and taboos, as modern man struggles to confront and control his inner demons. Musically and lyrically this is SJ's most varied album to date, ranging from harsh electronic onslaughts to a new kind of musical oblivion. Production and sound values are closer to industrial music than ever before, creating a very different feel to their previous filthwork "Pigdaddy". Enter if you dare, the very twisted and real world of Sutcliffe Jugend as they execute With Extreme Prejudice."
